newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: FEATURE-El Dorado dream no reality for Venezuela miners.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-El Dorado dream no reality for Venezuela miners.

text.p: Electricity is out again in the City of Gold, a dusty mining town in southeastern Venezuela with no water and a ramshackle strip of zinc-roofed houses along the pot-holed main street.

El Dorado, the dream of limitless riches that first drew European adventurers to the New World, runs into the real world here, 30 feet (10 metres) down a hand-dug mine, where miners scrape at soft rock with short-handled shovels. "Nothing, nothing, we have nothing here," sighed 50-year-old Nancy Montoya, owner of a general store in the town of 5,000.

Ciudad Dorada, the City of Gold, lies some 310 miles (500 km) south of the Caribbean coast, at the place marked with a treasure hunter's "X" in the yellowing maps of 16th century English explorer Sir Walter Raleigh.

Raleigh took no equipment, not even a pick, on his failed quests up the Orinoco river for El Dorado 400 years ago. In his imagination, the gold lay in ingots on the streets of a fabulous city, not in the ground at an average rate of 0.03 ounce (one gram) in a tonne of dirt.

In one of the desolate clearings where mining has despoiled the once-lush jungle around the town, Miguel Goy is lowered by rope down a deep but narrow mine shaft. A small-time prospector in his mid-40s with a barrel chest and powerful shoulders, he crouches at the bottom with a candle, then crawls under rough wooden props into an almost airless chamber little bigger than a grave.

His shift is typically eight hours. The day's six sacks of gold-bearing quartz -- called "white spar" by Raleigh -- are then carted off in a jalopy truck, ground and mixed with mercury to separate out the precious metal. With his two team-mates, "we get about six grams a day," he said. That is worth about $20, from which the mill takes its 25 percent cut.
A DREAM OF RICHES AND LUXURY

As a destination, little is heard of El Dorado after the end of the 16th century, although a scruffy mining town 45 miles (70 km) north of Ciudad Dorada bears that name. But the idea lived on as a folk memory, with its dream of riches, luxury and exotic obsessions.

Luis Chiquito ranks a few notches up from Ciudad Dorado's miners on the prospecting ladder. He is treasurer of a cooperative that brings drills, pumps and generators in helicopters to the nearby Nuevo Callao mine.
"No one pays attention to the idea of El Dorado around here," he said, sitting in the shade of a tree, whisky glass in hand. "Everyone knows there's gold, you just have to dig hard for it."

The Nuevo Callao mine is one of many illegal gold strikes that lie either side of the single good road that cuts 500 miles (800 km) south through Venezuela's eastern forests and high savanna all the way to Brazil. Some are carved out of jungle, others taken from concessions granted to foreign companies, the miners later evicted by the National Guard.

"Why should large companies only get the land when we've always been here and always mined?" asked Chiquito, whose conversation was peppered with the words "struggle" and "land" in an old-fashioned Latin American way. He resents the popular image of illegal mining towns as places rife with prostitution and heavy drinking. His, he said, even counts on a school and permanent paramedic paid for by the cooperative.
BIG COMPANIES ALSO SWEAT FOR GOLD

Prospectors have combed Venezuela's remote Bolivar state since the 1850s, when a German miner found a free-standing 15-pound (7 kg) gold nugget near present-day El Callao. By the early 1880s there were more than 8,000 settlers including English-speaking miners from nearby Guyana and Trinidad. English companies such as Monarch Resources and Greenwich Resources still have stakes in the area.

Las Cristinas, potentially the largest gold mine in Latin America, lies 40 miles (60 km) south of Nuevo Callao, next to Ciudad Dorada's holes-in-the-ground. But even this gold quest, a joint venture between Canada's Placer Dome and Venezuela's government, is proving a slog, the project stalled by a legal monster thrown up by Venezuela's Byzantine judicial system.

Rival company Crystallex says it owns the concession and has taken the case to the Supreme Court. "If Las Cristinas doesn't start soon we'll take the land by force and the National Guard will have to carry us out dead," fumed miner Orlando Eliseo, head of Ciudad Dorada's social affairs.
The village used to lie in Las Cristinas but was moved by the government in 1991. A fallen-down church and a statue of a miner and his dog still stand in the mine's long grass.

For a few years at the end of the 19th century, Venezuela was the world's premier gold producer, mining upwards of 17 tonnes per year, worth about $200 million at today's prices. Now it ranks around 17th with just 12 tonnes of officially registered production.
Local miners say the rest goes into the black market or other illegal channels such as laundering drug money.

The stalled Cristinas mine is the floundering flagship of the government's mining opening. Five years ago, more than 70 mining companies rushed in, but most have since retired as international gold prices plummeted, their mining applications got lost in Venezuela's almost impenetrable bureaucracy or their concessions were over-run by small miners.
"El Dorado is not in Venezuela," one frustrated mining executive said. "It's in Nevada."
